I'm not anti-ai but I am firmly anti-make-people-read-llm-output-I-didn't-read-myself, and this breaks this.

They also have a reward system that punishes people for ignoring the llm review (by pushing their submission lower in the queue).

> I'm not anti-ai but I am firmly anti-make-people-read-llm-output-I-didn't-read-myself, and this breaks this.

This here might hit the nail on the head exactly in terms of what the biggest FOSSes gripe with LLMs with might be: not the fact people use it but rather how it hinders the communication.

If you use it to help the write code, but you explain things in your own words or, at very least, redact and trim LLMs output, it's fine.

If you, however, just drop a wall of text at someone and expect they act on its b/s, this is lazy to the point it borders with microagression.

You wouldn't expect a distinguished professor explain basic maths to a student, and we shouldn't expect actual developers address Copilot's stupid, unredacted hallucinations or otherwise unrelated remarks.

This works for patches submission, too: you should be outright banned for submitting stuff you didn't bother to double check and properly document.

Maybe we should all respond to LLM text walls with aggressively doubled LLM text walls, expanding geometrically until the originating party either gives up or learns to communicate with their own words.

Dueling LLMs in your git repos means that you have nothing but dueling LLMs in your git repos.

It’s the LLM equivalent of “an eye for an eye just makes everyone blind”.

This is the short-term singularity, LLM agents endlessly conversing with another, just churning through tokens to throw noise at each other until it becomes a big ball of LLM turbolanguage.

Either some consensus emerges or it just deadlocks in place. My money is on the latter. I wish my money was in the companies profiting on it three years ago because that's the only way this will financially benefit people.
"An AI for an AI makes the world blind".

If you could explain what you're doing why would you use LLMs to do it in the fist place? For speed over control? Explaining means you're effectively able to do the modification yourself, and I'm fairly certain that's a low percentage of all AI contributions.
Same reason I can explain how to clean my house but I pay someone to do it? I want the end result, I don’t want to do the whole process myself.
No, most AI users who contributor to OS do not actually know what they're doing. Its a problem. And no amount of analogies about house keepers will change that.

That's the problem. We have a bunch of people who know how to do the work arguing about using LLMs to do it and assuming that all the submissions/reviews/etc are being done by people like them who know how to do the work.

Once you're drinking from the firehose you realize just how many idiots (well meaning or not) are out there, and how empowered they are now.

That is one of the biggest gripes for almost anyone I ever met who deals with AI generated content. Nobody really cares that someone else's work was generated with AI as much as they care that it's slop and they need to put in extra effort to work around the author's laziness.

Lazy or incompetent colleagues always forced people around them to overcompensate and correct. AI increased their firepower and blast radius.

But you just consume my slop with your Slopmaster 9000™, right?

The end-game for Anthropic is each PR to be 100k+ tokens but nobody cares because they burn 100k+ tokens reviewing and responding.

This is what we as consumers should look out for; what the tools built on top of LLMs try to do. Like it's neat that a tool can summon a dozen subagents with various models to churn out tasks, but if the task at hand is trivial then the amount of tokens used for it should be trivial.

We'll see the tools get adjusted over time to use more and more tokens, or at the very least they get optimized to use every paying customer's tokens for whatever period so that they are on the one side thinking they're getting their money's worth, or on the other that they should upgrade to a higher tier plan. Because the companies are investing trillions into thousands of datacenters and if they sit unused it'd have been a waste of money.

(the datacenters won't go unused I'm sure; any unused capacity will end up on a spot market, with cryptocurrency generation as a constant baseline. I'm pretty confident that crypto will make another small resurgence after the AI / datacenter investment bubble pops. This is a random internet comment, not financial advice)

"We're not forcing you to do your banking through our AI interface instead of a normal one, you're free to opt out, but multiple functions will be missing and we'll charge you a monthly fee."

If you’ve applied to jobs recently, you must have seen the companies that transcribe and summarize interviews using AI (and probably share data across their clients in an indirect, technically legal way).

You can opt out, of course, but do you really want to be the one candidate for which the interviewer needs to take notes manually? And they just spent a lot of money on this hiring AI tool, will they hire the one candidate for which they couldn’t use it?

So I've heard. I also know that several doctor's offices here use AI transcription. I'm sure I have a legal right to demand that they be switched off (I'm worried about privacy and accuracy here), but then I've got to be an asshole and increase the workload on my well-meaning doctor who probably had no say in any of this.

This is gonna get so much worse. It's like the smartphone revolution on steroids – and we've seemingly learned nothing! We're in dire straits.

I went through a lot of medical stuff a few months ago, and every single doctor asked me if they could use the device for that instead of typing it into the computer themselves. One of them explained that it allowed them to focus their whole attention on me, instead of partially on the computer for the inputting of the data while we talked.

I'm surprised that your doctors weren't asking, and instead were just assuming.
I don't believe they merely assume. If they don't ask in person, you've probably already opted in through patient check-in forms or the UI of a telehealth app.
I don't know if my doctor uses these systems. I don't go to my doctor very often. I've heard that many do, and I'm speculating.

> transcribe and summarize interviews using AI

That's cute. Yo, people be having full on AI-led interviews! That is to say, there's the human interviewee, and an AI, testing the human. Asking them questions and having a conversation that is definitely recorded.
The only way I would ever accept to be interviewed by an AI is if I was also allowed to have my AI assistant take the interview on my behalf.

I guess I have to temper my own statement a bit. I do see situations where I would generate and send automated LLM messages. Probably to reply to generated unsolicited messages or pull-requests.

But to upload to debian new's queue you already need to have pre-approval, it's a different situation from e.g. a public git repository that anyone can push to.

> where I would generate and send automated LLM messages. Probably to reply to generated unsolicited messages or pull-requests.

Why would you use an LLM instead of a fixed message?

To help classify between human and llm-generated ones? I don't know, and you're probably right than in this case a fixed message would be better.

Another situation where I would use llms to generate messages is if we've mutually agreed to do that. For example automated review messages at work, if we've agreed that it would be a part of our workflow.

A good rule of thumb might be unsolicited vs solicited llm messages.

Ok, for unattended replies indeed a fixed message is much better; you can't predict what an LLM will output, and a certain impersonal message is better than a personalized one that might be completely senseless.

If you mutually agreed of course it's fine

And even with a mutual agreement - default LLM output tends to be very hard and inefficient to read. We've spent quite a bit of time at work to setup a few writing skills for Claude.

For example, mine is a technical writing skill based on the old book "The Art of Scientific Writing": Front load information as much as possible - the first paragraph of a document should be a summary, the first sentence of a paragraph should summarize. Short sentences building on each other. Always show evidence.

Someone else spent quite a while optimizing a standardized PR description template, with a section for intent, expected changes, risk, rollout coordination and such.

That made the slop a lot more tolerable.

But there is also way to throttle that. Have AI go thru submission guidelines, compare it to PR and have it shut up when most (not all! AI will always give a reason if you ask it to check something) of it is correct, and only answer when the PR itself doesn't comply to the project rules

Yeah AI is the relevant stand in but ultimately this is about one group of people being lazy and trying to shift more work onto another group of people. It just so happens that they are using AI to do it
I don't think it "just so happens". AI enables that behavior at great scale and arguably even encourages it.

You can disagree with their approach, but I don't think it's fair to call the DFSG team, which is comprised of unpaid volunteers, "lazy". They have to vet every brand-new package that enters Debian, and their queue has an infamous history of being a bottleneck in the Debian project. Their time is certainly more valuable than the the time of the individuals uploading new packages.
I understand your confusion, but here's the truth of the matter: None of this has to be done. If anyone on the DFSG team does not want to do this work the answer is simple: Just don't do it.
How well is that working out for the chores at your house?
Do you not understand the difference between needs and wants?

Disclosure: I'm not a Debian Developer, yet I have worked on Debian derivatives and I'm somewhat familiar with internals of Debian from technical and human perspectives.

While I'm perfectly on the same page with the critics of the LLM generated summaries, I'm a bit torn on the issue.

For anyone not familiar with Debian ecosystem, there's a helper tool called Lintian. Lintian does all kinds of checks from package formatting, licenses to dependency management (which can detect both unnecessary yet included and necessary but missing dependencies via static analysis of your tool if necessary).

It's expected that your package to be "Lintian clean" to be able to included in Debian with minimum friction and wait. Even though it's Lintian clean, your package also checked by teams which are severely understaffed, and composed solely of voluntary people.

NEW queue also receives tremendous influx of packages (which can be considered a torrent, even). Since noon, there are 10 more ITP (intention to package) bugs open in my inbox.

As a result, at one hand, these people need every help they can get because getting new trainees and getting them to learn the intricacies is hard, on the other hand LLM generated text rightfully generate negative reactions from people. However, giving developers an automated check of what looks right and what looks wrong is helpful, in my perspective.

I wonder what people would have said it was a deterministic tool generating these reports and sending people these summaries as a "hey consider this feedback until a human has time to see your package".

This is a hard question and we need to think before impulsive reactions. I even don't have all or any of the answers, but at least I have some insight why this is there.
one of the points is that LLMs are NOT deterministic so you can't run them yourself a thousand times and expect the same output.

That's true, but if the LLM is calling a tool to provide the base information to extrapolate, the results will not change even if the sentence structure is never the same.

Debian has an extensive toolchain to check things. Having a set of deterministic tools which feed LLM with data can be beneficial, though.

Again, I'm not defending the LLM here, just want to show how hard the problem is to begin with.

And LLM "summarizes" the tool output as a completely unrelated and at times self-contradicting text.

If there are deterministic tools involved - just return their output as is. It's usually quite readable if needs a bit of adjusting

When was the last time you used a LLM?
This is not an issue with current models.

Maybe it's an unpopular opinion, but a concise report from one of today's frontier models is not something I would be offended by, even if nobody read it beforehand. I guess the fact that there is a nontrivial cost to it also eases the existential angst of neither being deterministic (Lintian) nor having been produced by a person.

Eh, you read compiler and linter output don't you? Nobody read that before you did.

Sure LLMs are not nearly as rigorous about their output but that doesn't mean it's entirely not useful.

At a minimum you can have your LLM summarize the other LLMs output and go from there.

Compiler output is somewhat deterministic and there is a logical path (even if caused by a compiler bug) and not dealing with it will definitely(!) lead to a broken product. Also at least I rarely read the full output, but I have an intuition, as the structure is consistent, what to look for in the output.

LLM output may or may not be relevant, may or may not tell me something new and by the way it is structure is often hard to quickly oarse for the relevant piece in a wall of text.

If I ask Claude to 'Review this PR' it will usually generate a very useful output and find bugs I wouldn't have spotted.

It does not have to be a wall of slop, maybe you only used LLMs 2 years ago where this would have been all you'd get.

It's disingenuous to compare LLM outputs to script generated ones. They have more differences than similarities.

A script is reproducible, and fixable. They won't waste your time hallucinating issues. Note that this is different from "being wrong". A script can be wrong, and you can spend time debugging it, but that time is not wasted. You can fix the script, remove wrong rules, whatever.

Also, nothing exists in a vacuum. Script-generated review comments were never a widespread societal issue, LLMs unfeterred content generation is.

It's a bit insane how it seems that "deterministic and reproducible", what I would consider to be a cornerstone of good software development, has apparently become an afterthought in the age of LLMs. All that for the sake of perceived convenience.

Not even convenience at times, I think that for some the amount of technical-sounding text LLMs can output on demand is comforting. It feels serious. It feels like it's doing something important.

Meanwhile the rest of us have to deal with these low-signal/high-noise walls of text in commit messages and PR comments. Or ask another LLM to summarize them, I suppose. "Doing and undoing, it's all work", as we say in French.

Devil's advocating here... is human code deterministic and reproducible? If I am assigned some non-trivial task, and write it twice with a week in-between, the code is not going to be identical, though it will meet the requirements. Or, if you give 3 different senior devs the same task on the same day, they will all be different, but still meet the requirements. What is different about asking an LLM to write code?

Well, for one thing, a human actually understands what he's doing. He isn't just generating something plausible based on statistics. As a result he makes fewer mistakes, can catch his own mistakes, and can learn from those mistakes.

> a human actually understands what he's doing. He isn't just generating something plausible based on statistics.

What makes you so sure that this is not the same thing?

Is the hallucination or “being wrong” the only major problem? Because if that’s the case I can’t imagine that problem will still be around in ~1-5 years.

I think it’s actually very similar to a script. It takes an input and produces an output. Certainly it has more variation than a traditional script, but it's generally going to return a very similar answer when the same input is given repeatedly, like when you ask an employee at a restaurant where the bathroom is. The verbiage may not be the same every time but the answer is always the same.

While I, like almost everyone, doesn't love reading LLM output, code review is an excellent use for LLMs. You know what I like less than reading LLM output?

- Slow PR review

- Nitpicks on style, not substance

- Async waiting for review or re-review after making changes, harder to stay in what passes for a "flow state" nowadays

- A lot of a ceremony around straightforward changes

We use LLM reviews at my company and it's caught things human reviews have not (as in in the early days we human-reviewed code and then did tests running the LLM afterwards and it caught things we didn't). It can review code at any time of the day and re-review it just as quickly as you can address the feedback.

I predict we (my company) are less than a year out from having a fully automated pipeline for reviews with only humans getting called in when it touches certain parts of the code. We already have a crude system for detecting certain file paths that we want a human to review if touched and we tweak that list over time as needed.

> Slow PR review

> Nitpicks on style, not substance

> Async waiting for review or re-review after making changes, harder to stay in what passes for a "flow state" nowadays

> A lot of a ceremony around straightforward changes

Those aren't great, but you what I like even less?

- Wall of nondeterministic bot text spam that may or may not be correct.

- Bot output has not been verified for correctness by the person who set up this bot output pipeline.

- Bot output has not even necessarily been read by the person who set it up.

- You have 24 hours to respond to this 5 page wall of text which may or may not be correct, or even make sense, or you will be penalized.

An appropriate response to this might be a reply flatly claiming that, actually, there aren't any problems after all, but that nobody has checked that that is true, and it is incumbent upon a human reviewer to verify your claims, like it was incumbent upon you to verify their bot's.

Can an LLM catch some errors? Absolutely. Can it be trusted to be correct absent review of the output? Absolutely not. So the simple solution seems to be, a human reviewer is free to run an LLM against code to review, on their own computer, and then they review the output, and they post the output only after verifying its correctness, taking personal responsibility for any issues with their posted output.

> Can an LLM catch some errors? Absolutely. Can it be trusted to be correct absent review of the output?

And the person that wrote the code is expected to be the review.

Unless it's an automated pipeline that fixes the things found - I'm not a fan of that unless it's made VERY clear the LLM needs to be VERY sure it's right. And even then, I'd prefer it go through a human to decide which things are valid, then send them off to be fixed.

Same here.LLMs are really good at code review providing they are configured correctly and have right docs and prompts.

Github copilot review is s great example of the worst possible way this can be misused. It is the worst waste of tokens there is.

Instead we use a process we created ourselves that runs opus or sonet (depending on complexity) to do a review (taking into account pr description and comments - copilot ignored those) and then to re-review the issues found to cut out BS.

This has been working very well mainly thanks to the prompts and docs we made it read, as well as us having lots of example code that shows how things should and should not be done.

One crappy thing Github does is that it doesn't allow our workflow based review's tokens to be accounted to individual PR authors like "copilot review" does, but accounts tokens to the organisation. It is obvious they are trying to herd people to using gh copilot review instead. But the quality difference is like night and day. So we are staying.

Agreed. It's sad how bad GH Copilot is, and thank you for reminding me to cancel that subscription. I just realized I haven't used it in a while now.

We also settled on a custom solution for reviews. We started with reviewers that claude/codex on GH actions and those were "ok" but kind of dumb and hard to tweak (GH Actions is just miserable to debug/iterate on). We still use them occasionally (@tag them to kick off a review) but we've shifted to a piece of software that we wrote that watches GH PRs and once certain labels have been added and the ticket in our ticket tracker (not GH issues) is marked as "Ready for Review" it kicks off a review and it reviews _all_ the PRs connected to the ticket. We don't have a monorepo, yet, so a new feature might span 3-4 repos (server, client1, client2, ...) and we want that work reviewed together.

We are close to having our review code spin up a fully isolated devstack running all our, many, services so it can poke around in the UI and write custom playwright scripts to test the new functionality. We have the devstack VMs working, just gluing the last of it together, it's pretty cool to see it all come together.

What about after the bot reviews, did you come up with any solutions to speed that up?
I’m talking about the human part of the review

We’re still experimenting. Automatically fixing obvious issues raised by the agent (at another agent’s discretion) or presenting a list of the feedback items with fix/refute suggestions are things we’ve toyed with.

Personally I have an agent review the feedback and break down each item so it’s easier to review (helps remove some of the jargon/short-hand that agents use sometimes). Then I decide what to have an agent address and what to push back on. Like I said, I’m working on finding a way to automate part of that but haven’t settled on one I like yet.

I’m having issues with agents not applying the rules to begin with, during both implementing and reviewing, it just reads the rules and choses to ignore them sometimes, adding more rules just makes this more likely to happen, and having review cycles can potentially get to a state where two agents talk nonstop and increase the slop I need to read instead of reducing it.

GR resulted in Proposal E, Choice 5: Responsible Use of Generative AI. Clearly stating: "Any such automated process should be overseen by a human who remains accountable for its behavior and output."

Does not respect the maintainer's time: DSFG uses an LLM to automate reviews. It auto-replies to submissions. There is an appeal process to theoretically handle errors.

The crux of polite LLM use is on whom the burden of the flood of generated output falls.

If you are the consumer of your automated output, all good. Say you generate a report and read it, the burden of inaccuracy or verbose output generated in seconds falls on you. Not only does this avoid wasting other people's time, you have the power to go fix the tool to stop wasting yours.

If the output goes directly to others, the burden of correcting inaccuracy falls on them. The burden of reading it falls on them. And they usually then have to scale some wall of automation to reach a human and convince them to fix it. Users subjected to this will be rightly pissed off.
